conclusion.justification: The report concludes that third-trimester tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) does reduce mother-to-child HBV transmission in women with high HBV DNA, explicitly supporting the claim and citing guidelines and trial evidence.
conclusion.label: endorses

report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is not false. The best interpretation is that third-trimester tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) *does reduce* residual mother-to-child HBV transmission among women with high HBV DNA, when added to standard infant immunoprophylaxis. This is why major guidance recommends it at a threshold of HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL, generally beginning at 28 weeks.

**Evidence behind the conclusion**

- Maternal viral load is a key risk factor: transmission and failure of infant vaccine prevention rise as maternal HBV DNA rises.  
  https://imj.ie/prevention-of-mother-to-child-transmission-in-patients-with-chronic-hepatitis-b-virus-infection-and-high-viral-loads/

- A pivotal randomized trial specifically studied TDF to prevent transmission in mothers with high viral load; subsequent clinical discussion of the two similar trials concluded that TDF was effective in this population.  
  https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/nejmoa1508660  
  https://imj.ie/prevention-of-mother-to-child-transmission-in-patients-with-chronic-hepatitis-b-virus-infection-and-high-viral-loads/

**Why someone might think it is false:** a separate, rigorous Thailand placebo-controlled trial started TDF at 28 weeks and gave infants hepatitis-B immune globulin at birth plus a very intensive vaccine schedule. In that setting, baseline transmission was already very low with infant prophylaxis, making an additional TDF benefit difficult to demonstrate. That result does **not** show TDF is ineffective in high-viremia pregnancies generally; it shows that its incremental benefit depends on baseline transmission risk and the effectiveness/timing of infant immunoprophylaxis.  
https://stacks.cdc.gov/view/cdc/53398

WHO nevertheless recommends TDF prophylaxis from week 28 through at least delivery for HBsAg-positive pregnant women with HBV DNA ≥200,000 IU/mL.  
https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/978-92-4-000270-8
